RWX.tech: Region with read, write and execute rights at the same time according to the kernel (mach_vm_region_recurse). On Apple Silicon an ordinary program cannot get such memory; it exists only as a JIT compiler region (MAP_JIT), where each thread switches between writing and executing.

X-PRIV.tech: Executable region without a file (proc_pidinfo PROC_PIDREGIONPATHINFO returns no path), outside the shared memory of system libraries (dyld shared cache).

ENT-X.tech: Entropy of the pages of an executable region, computed from bytes read with mach_vm_read_overwrite. Code of libraries in the system shared cache is not read.

HDR.tech: Mach-O header (magic 0xfeedfacf or 0xfeedface with a valid CPU and file type) at the start of a page in a region without a file; PE and ELF headers are searched for as on other systems.

THR-PRIV.tech: On macOS the scanner does not collect thread addresses yet, so this characteristic is not raised here; the description applies to results from other sources.

IMG-MOD.tech: On macOS the scanner does not compare code in memory with the file on disk yet, so this characteristic is not raised here; the description applies to results from other sources.

SHC.tech: Search in executable regions without a file: on arm64 the svc #0x80 instruction (a direct system call, which programs normally make only through the system library), on x86_64 the same patterns as on other systems.

combos.title: code from a file that looks packed
combos.meaning: A fragment of code loaded from a program or library file has very high entropy, that is, it looks like compressed or encrypted data. On macOS this feature on its own usually concerns code from a file: code with no file would also carry the X-PRIV feature.
benign: Cryptographic libraries, audio and video codecs and character conversion have large tables of constants in their code (seen in libgcrypt, libcrypto, libiconv and in multimedia libraries).
Large programs with resources compiled in, for example the Node.js runtime or native Python modules.
malicious: A packed program that decrypts its own code only after it starts.
A library in an application directory replaced with a version that hides a payload.

*.do: See what this region is in the memory map of the process
*.look: The result is one line: region type, address range, current and maximum permissions (for example r-x/rwx) and a file name if there is one. Benign case: a __TEXT line with the name of the program or of a library from /System or /usr/lib. An executable region (letter x) of type VM_ALLOCATE or without a file name should worry you: save it to a file (next step). No result: the region may be gone already.

*.do: Save the contents of the region to a file (requires lldb and root, pauses the process briefly)
*.look: A file /tmp/region-<pid>-<address>.bin with the bytes of the region is created. Inspect it with file and strings: names of network functions, URLs or shell commands in a region without a file need an explanation. An access error means the process is protected by the system (SIP or hardened runtime).

*.do: Check the signature of the program the process belongs to
*.look: A program from Apple or a known vendor has Authority lines with the publisher name and a TeamIdentifier. An adhoc signature or a missing TeamIdentifier on a program that claims to be a known product needs an explanation. flags containing runtime means a hardened runtime, where executable memory without a file is possible only with a permission recorded in the program's entitlements.

RWX.do: Check whether the program has the system's permission to generate code at run time
RWX.look: A line with allow-jit means a program with a JIT compiler (a browser, a JavaScript runtime, a virtual machine): a writable and executable region is normal for it. No result for a program with a hardened runtime means it should not have such a region. A program without a hardened runtime (adhoc signature, own build) can create a JIT region without this permission.

HDR.do: Count the program and library images that the system itself loaded into the process
HDR.look: The number shows how many images the system knows. A program header found in a region that is not among the __TEXT lines with a file name is an image loaded behind the system's back: save the region to a file (general steps) and inspect it with otool -l.

X-PRIV.do: Check whether the process contains a runtime that generates code at run time
X-PRIV.cmd: vmmap {pid} | grep -E "JavaScriptCore|Electron Framework|Chromium Embedded Framework|Google Chrome Framework|libnode|/node|libjvm|libcoreclr" | head -5
X-PRIV.look: Lines with the name of such a library mean a program with a JIT compiler: executable memory with no file is normal for it, usually in large regions. An empty result means none of the typical runtimes was found (the list is not complete) and the region is harder to explain: check the signature of the program and save the region to a file (general steps).

ENT-X.do: If the region comes from a file, check that the file has not been changed since it was signed; replace FILE with the file path from the region table
ENT-X.look: The result valid on disk and satisfies its Designated Requirement means the file is as it was signed. High entropy in the code of a cryptographic library, a codec or character conversion is then ordinary: these are tables of constants compiled into the code. Libraries from Homebrew and MacPorts carry a signature without a publisher (adhoc) and that is ordinary too. Be concerned about the message code object is not signed at all or invalid signature for a file of an application that claims to be a known product: in that case look up the hash from the second command in a file reputation database and keep the file. Save a region with no file to a file (general steps) and check it with the file and strings commands.

SHC.do: Disassemble the code before the address from the finding description (the address after the @ sign); replace ADDRESS with that address (needs lldb and root privileges, pauses the process briefly)
SHC.look: Look for a pair: mov x16 with a number (the call number) followed a few instructions later by svc #0x80. The number says what the code asks the kernel for: 59 starts a program (execve), 97 and 98 create and open a network connection, 74 changes memory permissions. Programs on macOS call the kernel through the system library, so such a pair in memory with no file is unusual even in a program with a JIT compiler. A benign explanation is a tool that builds its own system calls on purpose, for example an emulator or a security product. Otherwise save the region to a file (general steps) and hand it over for analysis.

terms.SIP: System Integrity Protection: the macOS protection that prevents even an administrator from reading the memory of system processes
terms.hardened runtime: a mode in which a program cannot have code outside its signed file or be debugged unless it carries a recorded permission
terms.dyld shared cache: one shared file with all system libraries, mapped into every process at the same address
terms.MAP_JIT: the flag of memory intended for a compiler that generates code while the program runs
terms.Mach-O: the format of program and library files on macOS
terms.task port: the handle through which the system allows reading the memory of another process; obtaining it requires privileges

flags.code signature: the state of the program's signature according to the kernel: whether it is valid, whether the program is a system one, whether it has a hardened runtime (then code outside the signed file needs a permission recorded in the entitlements)
flags.program entitlements: permissions recorded in the program's signature; allow-jit lets it generate code at run time, allow-unsigned-executable-memory and disable-executable-page-protection lift the protection of executable memory, get-task-allow lets other processes read this program's memory

processes.what: The first process of the system; it starts services and is the ancestor of all others.
Draws windows and drives the display; a system process protected by SIP.
The file manager and the user's desktop.
The Steam gaming platform client and its helper processes; it contains the Chromium browser engine, which generates code at run time.
GnuPG helper processes: they keep keys in memory, handle smart cards and key retrieval. Usually installed by MacPorts or Homebrew.
The Node.js runtime: it runs JavaScript programs and generates code at run time. It can be a separate installation or part of another application, so the file location has to be judged on its own.
The Python interpreter. What the process does depends on the script it runs: check the command line.

modules.what: the system loader; present in every process
Apple's JavaScript engine; generates code at run time
the Node.js runtime; generates code at run time
the Java virtual machine; generates code at run time
the Chromium browser engine (also in Electron applications); generates code at run time
modules.family: an application built on the Chromium browser engine (Electron, CEF or the browser itself): its interface is a web page shown by an embedded browser. It runs as several processes and generates code at run time.

modules.what: the .NET runtime; generates code at run time
cryptographic libraries; their code contains large tables of constants, hence the high entropy
character set conversion; the code contains large tables
the Chromium browser engine as shipped in Qt WebEngine; generates code at run time
modules.family: a program that uses Qt WebEngine: a Qt application that shows web content with an embedded Chromium engine. Pages are usually handled by a separate QtWebEngineProcess process, which generates code at run time.
